title: Tutorial
text:
Overview
This tutorial demonstrates how to use the NEO_Nature package to reproduce the core workflow of the project:

Cleaning and merging Near-Earth Object (NEO) and natural disaster data

Running exploratory analysis to examine potential relationships between asteroid characteristics and disaster occurrence

All analysis in this project is exploratory and does not claim causation.

title: Tutorial
text:
Setup
Before running this tutorial, make sure:

The repository has been cloned locally
Required packages (such as pandas) are installed
The data/ directory contains:

neo_data.csv
disaster_data.csv

title: Tutorial
text:
Running the Cleaning Pipeline
The cleaning pipeline loads the raw datasets, merges them by date, and saves a cleaned dataset for analysis.

from NEO_Nature.cleaning import run_cleaning_pipeline

run_cleaning_pipeline()

This step: - Reads the raw NEO and disaster datasets from data/ - Merges them on the date column - Saves the cleaned dataset to data/merged_neo_disaster_data.csv
You only need to run this step once unless the raw data changes.

title: Tutorial
text:
Running the Analysis Pipeline
After the merged dataset has been created, you can run the analysis pipeline.

from NEO_Nature.analysis import run_analysis_pipeline

run_analysis_pipeline()

This step: - Loads the merged dataset - Aggregates asteroid size and disaster counts by date - Computes correlations for: - Same-day asteroid size vs. disaster count - One-day lagged disaster counts - Hazardous asteroids only - Prints summary statistics and a conservative conclusion
The printed results correspond directly to the findings discussed in the final report.

title: Tutorial
text:
Expected Output
When run successfully, the analysis pipeline will print:

Correlation values for each comparison
A short, plain-language conclusion indicating whether meaningful relationships were detected

These results are intentionally summarized to support reproducibility and clarity.

title: Tutorial
text:
Notes

This tutorial prioritizes reproducibility over visualization
All exploratory plots and deeper investigation were conducted in NEO_eda.ipynb
The package structure allows the full workflow to be rerun without interacting with notebooks

title: Tutorial
text:
Conclusion
By running the cleaning and analysis pipelines shown above, users can fully reproduce the core results of the NEO-Nature project from raw data to final conclusions.

title: Written Report
text:
This project served as a valuable exercise in large-scale data retrieval, cleaning, and exploratory statistical analysis. It gave us the opportunity to engage with real scientific data and test a simple hypothesis about a topic that pushes beyond the boundaries of everyday analytics: the relationship between space-borne events and Earth-bound natural phenomena.
We began by surveying the range of available data sources. NASA provides a rich set of accessible APIs, covering everything from the Astronomy Picture of the Day to near-earth objects (NEOs), solar storms, and global climate observations. Because our goal was to identify whether activity in space might influence natural events on Earth, we decided to focus on NEO data alongside global weather and disaster event data. While we did not expect to establish causation, necessarily, any evidence of measurable correlation could motivate further research and potentially improve our predictions for dangerous environmental events. From this motivation, we developed three core research questions:

Do increases in asteroid fly-bys correspond with increases in natural disaster frequency?
If a relationship exists, are particular types of natural disasters more impacted than others?
Do NASA-classified “hazardous” NEOs show stronger correlation with natural disasters than non-hazardous ones?

After defining our questions, we pulled data directly from NASA’s APIs and merged the two datasets based on shared dates. The preprocessing stage involved formatting timestamps, filtering out missing observations, and ensuring event counts were aligned per day. Once the dataset was clean, we performed a series of correlation analyses across all major disaster categories: earthquakes, hurricanes, floods, wildfires, volcanic eruptions, and more.
Our findings were consistent and clear: there is effectively zero correlation between NEO activity and natural disasters on Earth. Even when isolating NASA-designated hazardous asteroids, there was no meaningful statistical relationship with any weather or geological event category. The only near-significance was in volcanic eruptions, but this was due to a very limited number of overlapping observations (only about seven matching dates) which makes any observed correlation unreliable. With a larger sample size, that effect would likely disappear completely.
There were also several limitations worth noting. Although NASA maintains a vast catalog of space data, the historical depth of their disaster-related dataset is currently restricted. We were only able to obtain roughly one year of matching weather-event records back to around August of 2024, which makes it difficult to analyze trends across multiple seasons or years. With more historical coverage, particularly for low-frequency events like volcanic eruptions, our ability to test these hypotheses would be much stronger. Additionally, a broader dataset could make it possible to explore other relationships (such as lagged effects) that our single-year dataset could not support very well.
In the end, our conclusion is straightforward: asteroid fly-bys, aka NEOs, whether hazardous or routine, show no statistical relationship with the frequency or type of natural disasters occurring on Earth. While this result may not uncover dramatic cosmic-climate interactions, it does help reinforce confidence in current scientific understanding: NEOs are not driving global climate or disaster patterns.
And honestly, that’s probably reassuring news for all of us.
